notes.meaning: Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain away from the crowds. He chose these three close disciples so there would be the legal number of witnesses to see His heavenly glory. These same three men would later witness His deep sorrow in the garden of Gethsemane.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Church tradition identifies this high mountain as Mount Tabor, where three churches were later built to remember the event.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars doubt Mount Tabor because a fortified Roman garrison sat on top of it, suggesting higher peaks like Mount Hermon or Mount Meron instead.

notes.meaning: Jesus was transfigured before them, which means His outward appearance changed completely. His face shone brightly like the sun and His clothes turned radiant white. His true divine majesty, which was normally hidden under His human body, briefly shone out in full view.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Orthodox theology teaches that the light seen on the mountain was the uncreated, eternal light of God Himself, showing human nature restored to its divine beauty.

notes.meaning: Moses and Elijah suddenly appeared and talked with Jesus. Moses represented the Law and Elijah represented the Prophets, proving that all Old Testament Scripture points to Jesus and is fulfilled in Him. Their living presence also proved that God's servants continue to live after physical death.

Peter offered to set up three shelters made of branches, one each for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah. He spoke out of joyful amazement and wanted to stay on the mountain in that heavenly moment. Without realizing it, his offer mistakenly placed Jesus on the same level as the two ancient prophets.

A bright cloud surrounded them, which was the visible sign of God's holy presence. God the Father spoke from the cloud, announcing that Jesus is His dearly loved Son who pleases Him fully. The Father commanded the disciples to listen to Jesus above all other teachers.

Hearing God's powerful voice filled the disciples with terror, and they dropped facedown on the ground. Jesus came near, reached out to touch them, and told them to stand up and not be afraid. His gentle touch and kind words restored their courage and calmed their fears.

When the disciples looked up, the cloud and the two prophets were gone, leaving only Jesus standing before them. This showed that the shadows of the old law had passed away and pointed to Christ alone as their final guide. Believers look to Jesus as the sole leader of their faith.

As they walked down the mountain, Jesus told the three men not to tell anyone about the vision until He rose from the dead. Hearing about His glory before His crucifixion would only confuse people and spark dangerous misunderstandings among the crowds. His resurrection would later make the meaning of His majesty crystal clear.

The disciples asked why the Jewish Bible teachers taught that Elijah had to return before the Messiah came. They had just seen Elijah appear and quickly vanish, which puzzled them. They wondered how that ancient prophecy was supposed to be fulfilled.

Jesus answered that the teachers were right to say Elijah comes first to restore all things. This work meant turning people's hearts back toward God and preparing the nation for the Savior. God's promise through the prophet Malachi was true and trustworthy.

Jesus explained that the promised Elijah had already come, but the people did not recognize him. Instead, the rulers treated him poorly and put him to death. In the exact same way, Jesus warned that He Himself would soon suffer at their hands.

The disciples finally realized that Jesus was talking about John the Baptist. John was not Elijah brought back from the dead, but he fulfilled the prophecy by preaching in the spirit and power of Elijah. His arrest and execution foreshadowed what would soon happen to Jesus.

When Jesus and the three disciples returned, a large crowd was waiting for them. A father pushed through the crowd, dropped to his knees before Jesus, and pleaded for help. He showed great respect and urgent need as he begged the Lord to help his family.

The father begged for mercy because his son had terrible seizures and suffered horribly. The attacks were so violent that the boy often collapsed directly into open fire or into deep water. The desperate father knew his boy's life was in constant danger without divine help.

The man had brought his son to the nine disciples who had stayed behind, but they could not heal him. Even though Jesus had earlier given them authority over unclean spirits, their efforts failed completely here. Their failure caused disappointment and opened the door for religious critics to argue with them.

Jesus called the generation faithless and twisted because they continued to doubt God despite seeing so many miracles. He felt the heavy burden of their spiritual stubbornness and asked how long He had to put up with them. Yet in His deep compassion, He ordered that the boy be brought directly to Him.

Jesus spoke with commanding authority to the demon that afflicted the boy. The evil spirit obeyed and left immediately, releasing its hold on the child. From that very second, the boy was completely healed and made whole.

Later, when they were alone in a house, the disciples asked Jesus why they had failed to cast out the demon. They were embarrassed and confused by their defeat before the crowd. They wanted to know why their spiritual power had not worked.

Jesus answered that they failed because their faith was far too weak. He told them that even faith as tiny as a mustard seed could tell a mountain to move, and it would obey. Genuine faith relies entirely on God's great power rather than human strength to overcome impossible hurdles.

This verse states that this stubborn kind of evil spirit leaves only through earnest prayer and fasting. Fasting means voluntarily skipping food to focus one's heart and mind fully on God. Going deep in spiritual devotion gives believers the close walk with God needed for tough spiritual battles.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The earliest and most reliable Greek manuscripts omit this verse entirely, suggesting an early copyist added it into Matthew from the parallel account in Mark 9:29.

notes.meaning: While gathering together in Galilee, Jesus warned His disciples that He would soon be betrayed into the hands of men who would kill Him. He comforted them by adding that He would rise back to life on the third day. The disciples were crushed with deep sorrow because they fixated on His coming death and did not yet understand the victory of His resurrection.

When they reached Capernaum, the local collectors of the temple tax approached Peter. This was not a Roman tax, but a yearly half-shekel contribution paid by Jewish men to maintain the temple and its worship in Jerusalem. They asked Peter whether his Teacher intended to pay what was customary.

Peter quickly answered yes and headed into the house. Before Peter could say a word, Jesus spoke first to show that He already knew all about the conversation. He asked Peter whether earthly kings demand taxes from their own children or from other citizens.

Peter answered that kings collect money from other people, leading Jesus to explain that the royal children are exempt, meaning free from paying. Because the temple belongs to God, Jesus is the Father's true Son and owes no tax to His Father's house. His royal divine identity meant He had no moral requirement to pay for the temple.

differ.view: Jesus and His disciples are all free from the temple tax because they are children of God, and Christ's kingdom replaces the old temple system.
Only Jesus Himself has natural royal exemption as the unique Son of God, and He keeps His status distinct from the disciples while gracious to them.

notes.meaning: Even though Jesus was free from the tax, He chose to pay so they would not offend the people or cause anyone to stumble. He sent Peter to catch a fish with a hook, saying the first fish would hold a four-drachma silver coin in its mouth to pay for both of them. This miracle revealed Christ's total rule over nature while showing His gentle humility to lay down His rights for the sake of peace.
